newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends higher as US stocks stage broad recovery.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends higher as US stocks stage broad recovery.

text.p: Wall Street stocks finished broadly higher, as buyers finally returned from the sidelines to send blue chips to their first significant rise in a week.
The Dow industrials rose 40 points to close unofficially at 6308, propelled by the top technology and financial names, the same stocks that fueled the fierce November rally.

"The old leaders are re-asserting themselves," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co. "We've essentially had a five percent correction without a fundamental change in the economy."
The Dow's top gainers included International Business Machines Corp, which rose 3-1/8 to 151-3/4, and J.P. Morgan & Co Inc, which gained 2-5/8 to 97-3/8.
Wall Street largely shrugged off news that the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee opted to leave interest rates unchanged, which analysts had considered a foregone conclusion.
"This was not exactly a roaring surprise," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "It was the non-event of the year."
With the Dow's losses exceeding 200 points over the last four sessions, analysts said stocks were starting to look like bargains.

"What we saw over the prior three or four days was a pretty significant underperformance," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan. "We had actually gotten to a point where stocks looked undervalued versus bonds."
Indeed, stocks were able to post their rally despite weakness in the bond market, where the 30-year U.S. Treasury lost 15/32 to 97-28/32, sending the yield up to 6.66 percent.

While the recovery was a welcome sign, the mood on Wall Street was far from exuberant. For the second straight session, a major investment firm -- this time the nation's largest -- voiced caution on the stock market's outlook.
At a press briefing to discuss their views on 1997, top strategists at Merrill Lynch predicted that next year, investors might be better served by holding bonds instead of stocks.
Merrill chief economist Donald Straszheim said the firm expected operating earnings among companies in the Standard & Poor's 500 index would rise only 2.5 percent next year.
"The equity markets are not going to have quite the tailwind of earnings," he said, noting the firm expects S&P 500 earnings growth of 6.1 percent in 1996.
Market volume remained very heavy, with nearly 520 million shares changing hands on the NYSE. Breadth was evenly divided, with advancing issues edging out decliners 1,246 to 1,240.

In individual issues, Frontier Corp fell 5-5/8 to 20-3/4 after warning its fourth quarter earnings would be below year-ago levels and consensus estimates. Frontier was the NYSE's most heavily traded issue.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 5.34 to 1266.32.
The S&P 500 rose 5.06 to 726.04.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
General Electric Co climbed 2-1/2 to 97-5/8, a day after chairman John Welch briefed analysts on the company's outlook.

A company spokesman declined to comment on Welch's remarks but analysts who attended the meeting described the presentation as upbeat. During his remarks, Welch expressed confidence GE would meet Wall Street earnings estimates for the 1996 calendar year, analysts said.
Stanford Telecommunications Inc jumped 4-1/8 to 29-3/4 after Oppenheimer & Co raised its rating on the shares to buy from market perform.
